verses.text: Now these were the sons of David, who were born to him in Hebron: the firstborn, Amnon, of Ahinoam the Jezreelitess; the second, Daniel, of Abigail the Carmelitess;
the third, Absalom the son of Maacah the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur; the fourth, Adonijah the son of Haggith;
the fifth, Shephatiah of Abital; the sixth, Ithream by Eglah his wife:
six were born to him in Hebron; and he reigned there seven years and six months. He reigned thirty-three years in Jerusalem;
and these were born to him in Jerusalem: Shimea, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon, four, of Bathshua the daughter of Ammiel;
and Ibhar, Elishama, Eliphelet,
Nogah, Nepheg, Japhia,
Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet, nine.
All these were the sons of David, besides the sons of the concubines; and Tamar was their sister.
Solomon’s son was Rehoboam, Abijah his son, Asa his son, Jehoshaphat his son,
Joram his son, Ahaziah his son, Joash his son,
Amaziah his son, Azariah his son, Jotham his son,
Ahaz his son, Hezekiah his son, Manasseh his son,
Amon his son, and Josiah his son.
The sons of Josiah: the firstborn Johanan, the second Jehoiakim, the third Zedekiah, and the fourth Shallum.
The sons of Jehoiakim: Jeconiah his son, and Zedekiah his son.
The sons of Jeconiah, the captive: Shealtiel his son,
Malchiram, Pedaiah, Shenazzar, Jekamiah, Hoshama, and Nedabiah.
The sons of Pedaiah: Zerubbabel and Shimei. The sons of Zerubbabel: Meshullam and Hananiah; and Shelomith was their sister;
and Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah, and Jushab Hesed, five.
The sons of Hananiah: Pelatiah and Jeshaiah; the sons of Rephaiah, the sons of Arnan, the sons of Obadiah, the sons of Shecaniah.
The son of Shecaniah: Shemaiah. The sons of Shemaiah: Hattush, Igal, Bariah, Neariah, and Shaphat, six.
The sons of Neariah: Elioenai, Hizkiah, and Azrikam, three.
The sons of Elioenai: Hodaviah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan, Delaiah, and Anani, seven.

footnotes.content: David's firstborn sons are set down by name and mother—each child a real person, not a cipher. Notice how the chronicler honors both son and mother, anchoring them in place: Amnon of Ahinoam the Jezreelitess. The Lord sees each child born, and so do we.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Absalom is named here as David's third son—the young man who would one day rise against his father. In this moment, though, he is simply listed: a child of Maacah, daughter of a foreign king. The Lord knew his end before his beginning.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The fifth and sixth sons complete the Hebron count. Eglah is named as David's wife here—a faithful presence in the record. Even in genealogy, the Lord honors the quiet faithfulness of those who stood beside the king.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven years and six months in Hebron; thirty-three in Jerusalem. These numbers frame David's reign in two halves—anointing in the south, then the capital secured in the north. The Lord measured his days in seasons.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon is born in Jerusalem—son of Bathshua (called Bathsheba in other places). Here again, the chronicler names the mother alongside the children. From a union born in shadow came a son who would build the Lord's house. Grace works in ways we do not always see at first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three more sons, each with his own thread in the tapestry. Eliphelet appears twice in this listing—a name that echoes, yet points to different men. Even in a simple list, the Lord's people multiply and branch.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three more sons, names bright and particular. Nogah means 'shining'; Nepheg, 'sprout.' Even in genealogy, the Lord's naming shows care—each child a gift, each name a small prayer spoken over his life.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Nine sons born in Jerusalem—a full number, a sign of blessing. Yet not all of them walked quietly into what the Lord had for them. Some would stumble; the Lord's grace would reach them still.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Tamar is named here—David's daughter, sister to all these sons. Her presence in the record matters; the chronicler will not let her fade. In a house of men, the Lord honors the daughters too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Solomon's line begins: Rehoboam, Abijah, Asa, Jehoshaphat—a chain of kings stretching forward from David's son. Yet not all of them walked faithfully. The throne is passed, but it does not guarantee the heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joram, Ahaziah, Joash—the line continues. Some of these kings would do what is right; others would turn their faces from the Lord. Yet still He did not abandon the covenant with David.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Amaziah, Azariah, Jotham—three more names in the succession. Azariah (also called Uzziah) would reach great strength, then pride would bring him low. The Lord's mercy endures even when we forget our need for Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahaz, Hezekiah, Manasseh—each a reign, each a test. Hezekiah especially sought the Lord's face in desperate hour; Manasseh would stumble into grave darkness before finding his way home. Even a king cannot hide from grace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Amon, Josiah—the line moves toward exile. Josiah will be the last good king of Judah, and after him, the kingdom fractures. Yet even in the shadow of coming judgment, the Lord's faithfulness does not waver.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Four sons of Josiah are named—Johanan first, then Jehoiakim, Zedekiah, Shallum. None of them will inherit undivided peace. Yet the Lord sees each son, each struggle, each attempt to hold the kingdom together.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jehoiakim's line—Jeconiah, who will be called the captive. The names grow heavier now; we feel the weight of exile drawing near. Yet the Lord does not abandon His covenant even when His people are carried away.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shealtiel, son of Jeconiah the captive—this name marks a turning. Shealtiel means 'I have asked God.' In exile, a child is born; hope begins to stir again. The line does not end; it bends toward home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Five sons of Jeconiah the captive are named—sons born into exile, yet sons nonetheless. Shenazzar especially will have a role to play in the return. Even captivity does not silence the Lord's purposes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zerubbabel emerges—the one who will lead the return and lay the temple's foundation anew. Shelomith is named as his sister; her place is kept in the record. The Lord honors the faithful, whether they stand in the temple's light or in the shadow.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Five grandsons of Zerubbabel—the line multiplies again in exile's aftermath. Each name represents a family continuing, a thread still held. The captivity is not the end; it is a turn in the road.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The genealogy spreads into branches—Hananiah's line, Rephaiah's, Arnan's, others. These names may be less known, yet each represents a family that continued the faith through exile and return. Faithfulness often wears a humble face.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shecaniah's son Shemaiah, and his six sons—the line still branches. Six sons means blessing; they will become fathers and grandfathers themselves. The Lord's people multiply even when history forgets their names.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Neariah's three sons close out one branch. Three sons, three carriers of the name forward. How many of David's line survived the exile? Only the Lord knows; yet enough to fulfill His promise, and enough to lead us toward the Messiah.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven sons of Elioenai—a full number again, blessing renewed. Readers today hear an echo: through all the exile, all the forgetting, all the years when it seemed the covenant had broken, the Lord held fast. His line endured. That should comfort us now.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
